metadata.title: Week 7 KP01 Weight initialization (guided version)
metadata.description: IDL 2026 Week 7 KP01; reasoning-led-teaching-deck 2.1; English, self-paced reading; manual advance, try before reveal

p01-start-title.name: p01-start-title
p01-start-title.text: Where do the numbers in a convolution kernel come from at the first step?

p01-start-ctx.name: p01-start-ctx
p01-start-ctx.text: Week 6 finished the parts of a convolutional layer. This unit returns to a more basic question: what should the numbers in the kernel be before training starts?

p01-start-kt.name: p01-start-kt
p01-start-kt.text: A sample $3\times3$ convolution kernel $W$ (values are [Added] illustrations)

p01-start-need-t.name: p01-start-need-t
p01-start-need-t.text: Training = backpropagation: first compute the gradient of the loss $L$ with respect to every weight, then take a small step against it. Every step starts from the 'current weights'.

p01-start-upd-t.name: p01-start-upd-t
p01-start-upd-t.text:
$W^{(t+1)}=W^{(t)}-\eta\,\nabla_W L\bigl(W^{(t)}\bigr)$
Before the first step there is no $W^{(0)}$ and the formula cannot be evaluated — so every weight must first have a number.

p01-start-routes-t.name: p01-start-routes-t
p01-start-routes-t.text:
Three routes:
1. random initialization (break symmetry)　2. variance-aware random methods: Xavier, He (set the size)　3. an unsupervised method that first learns a set of kernels: PCA
Modern practice relies mainly on the first two. This unit answers in turn: why random? how large? why is random usable?

p02-sym-forward-title.name: p02-sym-forward-title
p02-sym-forward-title.text: Two neurons — why do they do only one neuron's work?

p02-sym-forward-ctx.name: p02-sym-forward-ctx
p02-sym-forward-ctx.text: The easiest idea: set everything to the same number. Small network: input $x=(1,2)$, two ReLU hidden neurons, one output, target $t=3$, all weights $0.5$ ([Added]).

p02-sym-forward-c3-t.name: p02-sym-forward-c3-t
p02-sym-forward-c3-t.text: Adding two identical hidden outputs creates no new feature direction.

p03-sym-backward-title.name: p03-sym-backward-title
p03-sym-backward-title.text: The gradients are identical — can the update break the symmetry by itself?

p03-sym-backward-ctx.name: p03-sym-backward-ctx
p03-sym-backward-ctx.text: Continuing the previous page: $h_1=h_2=1.5$, $y=1.5$, $t=3$, loss $\tfrac12(y-t)^2$. The first thing in backpropagation is the shared output error.

p03-sym-backward-g3-t.name: p03-sym-backward-g3-t
p03-sym-backward-g3-t.text: The same initial value minus the same gradient is still the same after the update, and the next step again receives the same gradient.

p04-zero-title.name: p04-zero-title
p04-zero-title.text: If everything is set to 0, does the network move?

p04-zero-ctx.name: p04-zero-ctx
p04-zero-ctx.text: The same small network, but now every weight is $0$ ([Added]; convention $\mathrm{ReLU}'(0)=0$).

p04-zero-z2-t.name: p04-zero-z2-t
p04-zero-z2-t.text:
Output-weight gradient $=e\,h=0$ (multiplied by the zero hidden output)
input-weight gradient $=0$ (multiplied by the zero output weight)

p04-zero-z3-t.name: p04-zero-z3-t
p04-zero-z3-t.text: The loss is not 0 but every gradient is: not a single step is possible. The remedy: make every weight start differently — use random numbers.

p05-practice-sym-title.name: p05-practice-sym-title
p05-practice-sym-title.text: Your turn: is it enough to make only the two neurons' input weights different?

p05-practice-sym-ctx.name: p05-practice-sym-ctx
p05-practice-sym-ctx.text: Change the hidden neurons' input weights to $(0.5,0.5)$ and $(0.3,0.7)$; the output weights are still all $0.5$. Think first, then check.

p05-practice-sym-q-t.name: p05-practice-sym-q-t
p05-practice-sym-q-t.text:
1. In this step, are the gradients of the two output weights equal?
2. Are the gradients of the two neurons' input weights equal?
3. After the update, will they still be equal at the next step?
4. What is the simplest way to avoid symmetry?

p05-practice-sym-a1-t.name: p05-practice-sym-a1-t
p05-practice-sym-a1-t.text:
$h=(1.5,\ 1.7)$, $y=0.5\times1.5+0.5\times1.7=1.6$, error $-1.4$.
Output-weight gradients $-2.1$ and $-2.38$: not equal.

p05-practice-sym-a2-t.name: p05-practice-sym-a2-t
p05-practice-sym-a2-t.text: Both input-weight gradients are $-1.4\times0.5\times(1,2)=(-0.7,-1.4)$: equal (because the output weights are still both $0.5$).

p05-practice-sym-a3-t.name: p05-practice-sym-a3-t
p05-practice-sym-a3-t.text:
After the update the two output weights differ, and only then do the input-weight gradients diverge at the next step; the two neurons stop being copies.
The simplest way: use random numbers for every weight and set the standard deviation by Section 4.

p06-variance-title.name: p06-variance-title
p06-variance-title.text: First a tool: how does variance scale and add?

p06-variance-ctx.name: p06-variance-ctx
p06-variance-ctx.text: Variance $\mathrm{Var}(X)$ measures how far a random number is from its mean. The two rules below are tools for the derivations ([Added]).

p06-variance-r1-t.name: p06-variance-r1-t
p06-variance-r1-t.text:
$\mathrm{Var}(aX)=a^{2}\,\mathrm{Var}(X)$
multiply by $a$ and the variance is multiplied by $a^{2}$.

p06-variance-r2-t.name: p06-variance-r2-t
p06-variance-r2-t.text:
$\mathrm{Var}(X+Y)=\mathrm{Var}(X)+\mathrm{Var}(Y)$ ($X,Y$ independent)
the variances of independent random numbers add.

p06-variance-warn-t.name: p06-variance-warn-t
p06-variance-warn-t.text: The two operations differ: enlarging the 'same' variable multiplies by $a^{2}$; adding 'another independent' variable adds variances.

p07-selftest-title.name: p07-selftest-title
p07-selftest-title.text: Your turn: three quick self-test questions

p07-selftest-ctx.name: p07-selftest-ctx
p07-selftest-ctx.text: All three are prerequisites used later. Think first, then check.

p07-selftest-q1-t.name: p07-selftest-q1-t
p07-selftest-q1-t.text: 1. If the variance of $X$ is $2$, what is the variance of $5X$?

p07-selftest-q2-t.name: p07-selftest-q2-t
p07-selftest-q2-t.text: 2. What is the definition of ReLU?

p07-selftest-q3-t.name: p07-selftest-q3-t
p07-selftest-q3-t.text: 3. Which rule does backpropagation use to pass the error from the output back through the layers?

p08-rms-title.name: p08-rms-title
p08-rms-title.text: How large is the signal? First separate rms from variance

p08-rms-ctx.name: p08-rms-ctx
p08-rms-ctx.text: The most direct way to see the effect of the initial values is to let a signal pass through the network and measure how large each layer's output is. This unit uses the root mean square, rms.

p08-rms-d1-t.name: p08-rms-d1-t
p08-rms-d1-t.text:
$\mathrm{rms}(x)=\sqrt{q}$, where $q=$ the mean of the squares (expectation).
The mean is not subtracted first.

p08-rms-d2-t.name: p08-rms-d2-t
p08-rms-d2-t.text:
$\mathrm{Var}(x)=q-\bigl(\mathbb{E}[x]\bigr)^{2}$
only when the mean is $0$ is the variance equal to $q$.

p08-rms-e-h.name: p08-rms-e-h
p08-rms-e-h.text: The same numbers, two different quantities

p08-rms-w-t.name: p08-rms-w-t
p08-rms-w-t.text: The mean of outputs after ReLU is often not $0$, so this unit tracks rms (the mean of squares) and does not claim that the variance is exactly halved.

p09-linear-title.name: p09-linear-title
p09-linear-title.text: How does a weighted sum accumulate the squared size of the signal?

p09-linear-ctx.name: p09-linear-ctx
p09-linear-ctx.text: One output multiplies $n$ inputs by different weights and adds them: $z=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_ix_i$. The weights are independent, with mean $0$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.

p09-linear-s2-t.name: p09-linear-s2-t
p09-linear-s2-t.text: Expectation of one term: $\mathbb{E}[w_i^{2}x_i^{2}]=\sigma^{2}q$ ($q$ = mean of the squares of the inputs).

p09-linear-s3-t.name: p09-linear-s3-t
p09-linear-s3-t.text: Different weights are independent with mean $0$, so the expectation of cross terms is cancelled by a zero factor: $\mathbb{E}[w_iw_j]=0$.

p09-linear-s5-t.name: p09-linear-s5-t
p09-linear-s5-t.text: So without an activation function the squared size of the output = the squared size of the input $\times\,n\sigma^{2}$.

p10-relu-half-title.name: p10-relu-half-title
p10-relu-half-title.text: ReLU cuts away half — which quantity is cut?

p10-relu-half-ctx.name: p10-relu-half-ctx
p10-relu-half-ctx.text: The weights are symmetrically distributed, so $z$ is symmetric in sign: a pair $\pm z$ has the same squared size. ReLU turns the negative half into $0$.

p10-relu-half-f-t.name: p10-relu-half-f-t
p10-relu-half-f-t.text:
The mean of squares is halved:
$\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{ReLU}(z)^{2}]=\tfrac12\,\mathbb{E}[z^{2}]=\tfrac12\,n\sigma^{2}q$

p10-relu-half-k-t.name: p10-relu-half-k-t
p10-relu-half-k-t.text:
Taking the square root gives the rms factor of one ReLU layer:
$\sqrt{\dfrac{n}{2}}\;\sigma$

p10-relu-half-note-t.name: p10-relu-half-note-t
p10-relu-half-note-t.text: Note: what is cut is half of the 'squared quantity', not an exact halving of the variance (the mean after ReLU is not $0$).

p11-factor-numbers-title.name: p11-factor-numbers-title
p11-factor-numbers-title.text: The factor in numbers: ten layers differ by a dozen orders of magnitude

p11-factor-numbers-ctx.name: p11-factor-numbers-ctx
p11-factor-numbers-ctx.text: $n=100$; after ten layers the rms is the input times 'the factor to the tenth power'. Experiment: a 10-layer fully connected ReLU network of width 100, Gaussian weights, 1000 standard-normal inputs ([Added], fixed seed).

p11-factor-numbers-why-t.name: p11-factor-numbers-why-t
p11-factor-numbers-why-t.text:
Each layer differs only by a fixed factor, and ten layers multiplied differ by a dozen orders of magnitude: $0.0707^{10}\approx3.1\times10^{-12}$ versus $7.07^{10}\approx3.1\times10^{8}$.
Theory and experiment are of the same order (a small gap arises because the assumptions do not hold exactly; see 'Going deeper').

p11-factor-numbers-goal-t.name: p11-factor-numbers-goal-t
p11-factor-numbers-goal-t.text: To keep the signal size, the factor per layer must be about $1$.

p12-relu-chart-title.name: p12-relu-chart-title
p12-relu-chart-title.text: Same random numbers, only the size changed: how far apart after ten layers?

p12-relu-chart-ctx.name: p12-relu-chart-ctx
p12-relu-chart-ctx.text: The vertical axis is logarithmic, each step is 10×; the green line is 1 (the reasonable range). ReLU, width 100 per layer.

p12-relu-chart-t4-t.name: p12-relu-chart-t4-t
p12-relu-chart-t4-t.text:
Blue: Xavier, $\sigma=0.1$
layer 10 $0.039$, still shrinking layer by layer

p13-tanh-title.name: p13-tanh-title
p13-tanh-title.text: tanh does not blow up — can its gradient still become small?

p13-tanh-ctx.name: p13-tanh-ctx
p13-tanh-ctx.text: The output of tanh is squeezed between $-1$ and $1$, so $\sigma=1$ does not blow up but sticks near $0.96$. Input standard deviation $0.1$ (so that tanh starts in its nearly linear range).

p13-tanh-satt.name: p13-tanh-satt
p13-tanh-satt.text: Far from the origin the curve flattens: output near 1, derivative near 0

p13-tanh-n1-t.name: p13-tanh-n1-t
p13-tanh-n1-t.text: A squeezed output does not mean the gradient can pass: in the flat part $\tanh'(z)\approx0$, and the backpropagated gradient is again almost zero.

p13-tanh-n3-t.name: p13-tanh-n3-t
p13-tanh-n3-t.text:
Blue: Xavier with tanh
after ten layers $\mathrm{rms}=0.095$ (start $0.1$), almost unchanged

p14-vanish-title.name: p14-vanish-title
p14-vanish-title.text: The gradient also passes through the same chain of layers: vanishing and exploding

p14-vanish-ctx.name: p14-vanish-ctx
p14-vanish-ctx.text: There is only one criterion: is the per-layer factor smaller than 1, equal to 1, or larger than 1?

p14-vanish-vt.name: p14-vanish-vt
p14-vanish-vt.text: Factor < 1: the signal shrinks layer by layer (vanishing)

p14-vanish-xt.name: p14-vanish-xt
p14-vanish-xt.text: Factor > 1: the signal grows layer by layer (exploding)

p14-vanish-cap.name: p14-vanish-cap
p14-vanish-cap.text: (The circle sizes only suggest how the 'signal size' changes; they are not drawn to scale.)

p14-vanish-b1-t.name: p14-vanish-b1-t
p14-vanish-b1-t.text: A forward signal shrunk to zero → the backward gradient shrinks to zero with it: the early layers hardly learn (vanishing gradient).

p14-vanish-b2-t.name: p14-vanish-b2-t
p14-vanish-b2-t.text: A forward signal that blows up → the gradient blows up too: one step pushes the weights out of control (exploding gradient).

p14-vanish-mis-t.name: p14-vanish-mis-t
p14-vanish-mis-t.text:
Thinking 'the larger the weights the better, to avoid vanishing'.
Too large also blows up; tanh and sigmoid are pushed into the flat part and the gradient is again almost zero.

p15-practice-factor-title.name: p15-practice-factor-title
p15-practice-factor-title.text: Your turn: with σ = 0.05, how much is left after ten layers?

p15-practice-factor-ctx.name: p15-practice-factor-ctx
p15-practice-factor-ctx.text: A ReLU network with $n=100$. Work it out, then check.

p15-practice-factor-q-t.name: p15-practice-factor-q-t
p15-practice-factor-q-t.text:
Weight standard deviation $\sigma=0.05$.
1. What is the factor per layer?
2. After ten layers, by how many times has the rms changed?
3. Is it vanishing or exploding?

p15-practice-factor-a3-t.name: p15-practice-factor-a3-t
p15-practice-factor-a3-t.text: The factor is smaller than $1$, so each layer shrinks: it is vanishing; the rms shrinks to about one thirty-thousandth.

p16-projection-title.name: p16-projection-title
p16-projection-title.text: What structure of the data does a random layer keep?

p16-projection-ctx.name: p16-projection-ctx
p16-projection-ctx.text: The weights $W$ of a layer are a matrix mapping the input to another vector, which is a linear projection. Random initialization = picking a projection at random.

p16-projection-dist-t.name: p16-projection-dist-t
p16-projection-dist-t.text:
The difference vector is also multiplied by the same matrix:
$u_a-u_b=W(x_a-x_b)$
distance: $\|W(x_a-x_b)\|_2$

p16-projection-scale-t.name: p16-projection-scale-t
p16-projection-scale-t.text:
Worry: could a randomly picked projection destroy the structure of the input?
Each entry of $W$ is Gaussian with mean $0$ and variance $1/k$, so that distances neither grow nor shrink overall.

p16-projection-same-t.name: p16-projection-same-t
p16-projection-same-t.text: Both points are multiplied by the same $W$: one cannot draw a separate matrix for each point.

p17-jl-title.name: p17-jl-title
p17-jl-title.text: The guarantee of the JL lemma: distance and squared distance must not be mixed

p17-jl-ctx.name: p17-jl-ctx
p17-jl-ctx.text: JL lemma: project $N$ points of $d$ dimensions to $k$ dimensions with a random matrix; if $k$ is large enough, any pairwise distance changes with high probability by only a bounded small fraction.

p17-jl-sq-h.name: p17-jl-sq-h
p17-jl-sq-h.text: The lemma speaks of squared distance

p17-jl-sq-t.name: p17-jl-sq-t
p17-jl-sq-t.text: The lemma says: the squared distance of any two points changes by no more than a factor $1\pm\varepsilon$, and $k$ is of order $\ln N/\varepsilon^{2}$ (only the order is stated).

p17-jl-rt-t.name: p17-jl-rt-t
p17-jl-rt-t.text: The experiment measures the distance itself: if the squared distance changes by $1\pm\varepsilon$, the distance changes by about $1\pm\varepsilon/2$ [Added].

p17-jl-exp-t.name: p17-jl-exp-t
p17-jl-exp-t.text: Experiment [Added]: $50$ points, $d=1000$, $1225$ pairwise distances. Project to $k=10,50,100,400$ dimensions and see by what percentage the worst pair changed.

p17-jl-trend-t.name: p17-jl-trend-t
p17-jl-trend-t.text: Trend: the error shrinks as $k$ grows, and no pair of distances is turned unrecognizable.

p18-he-title.name: p18-he-title
p18-he-title.text: Set the factor to 1 and derive He initialization

p18-he-ctx.name: p18-he-ctx
p18-he-ctx.text: JL says 'random' is feasible; now we answer how to set the 'size'. The previous section derived that the factor of one ReLU layer is $\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{in}}/2}\,\sigma$.

p18-he-s1-t.name: p18-he-s1-t
p18-he-s1-t.text:
Goal: output as large as input, i.e. the factor equals $1$:
$\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{in}}/2}\;\sigma=1$

p18-he-s2-t.name: p18-he-s2-t
p18-he-s2-t.text:
Solve for $\sigma$:
$\sigma_{\mathrm{He}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{n_{\mathrm{in}}}}$ (for ReLU and its variants)

p18-he-s3-t.name: p18-he-s3-t
p18-he-s3-t.text:
$n=100$: $\sigma_{\mathrm{He}}=\sqrt{2/100}=0.141$.
$n_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the number of inputs of each neuron (fan-in).

p18-he-s4-t.name: p18-he-s4-t
p18-he-s4-t.text: The green line (layer-by-layer figure): over ten layers the rms lies between $1.00$ and $1.62$, and at layer 10 it is $1.24$.

p18-he-s5-t.name: p18-he-s5-t
p18-he-s5-t.text:
Keep the standard deviation $\sigma$ and the variance $\sigma^{2}$ apart: the formula uses the standard deviation.
It is not an exact guarantee: the derivation assumes independent layer inputs, zero-mean weights and no biases (see 'Going deeper').

p19-xavier-title.name: p19-xavier-title
p19-xavier-title.text: Why does Xavier look at both fan-in and fan-out?

p19-xavier-ctx.name: p19-xavier-ctx
p19-xavier-ctx.text: Xavier (Glorot) initialization goes with saturating activation functions such as tanh and sigmoid.

p19-xavier-f-t.name: p19-xavier-f-t
p19-xavier-f-t.text:
Nearly linear, without ReLU's halving:
factor per layer $\sqrt{n_{\mathrm{in}}}\,\sigma=1$ → $\sigma^{2}=1/n_{\mathrm{in}}$.

p19-xavier-b-t.name: p19-xavier-b-t
p19-xavier-b-t.text:
The gradient passes through the fan-out $n_{\mathrm{out}}$ (how many neurons a neuron sends its signal to):
backward needs $\sigma^{2}=1/n_{\mathrm{out}}$.

p19-xavier-x-t.name: p19-xavier-x-t
p19-xavier-x-t.text: Compromise [Added]: $\sigma_{\mathrm{Xavier}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{n_{\mathrm{in}}+n_{\mathrm{out}}}}$ (take the reciprocals of the two ideal variances, average, and take the reciprocal again)

p20-pairing-title.name: p20-pairing-title
p20-pairing-title.text: Pairing matters: who goes with whom?

p20-pairing-ctx.name: p20-pairing-ctx
p20-pairing-ctx.text: Fix the network and the scale and compare initializations and activation functions. Xavier and He target different activation functions.

p20-pairing-c12-t.name: p20-pairing-c12-t
p20-pairing-c12-t.text: Factor about $\sqrt2$, growing each layer; tanh is easily pushed to the flat part [Added] (experiment layer 10: $0.54$)

p20-pairing-c21-t.name: p20-pairing-c21-t
p20-pairing-c21-t.text: Factor $1/\sqrt2=0.707$, after ten layers $0.707^{10}=0.031$; experiment $0.039$, slowly shrinking

p20-pairing-c22-t.name: p20-pairing-c22-t
p20-pairing-c22-t.text: Matched ✓ after ten layers $\mathrm{rms}=0.095$, start $0.1$, almost unchanged

p20-pairing-wr.name: p20-pairing-wr
p20-pairing-wr.text: Common error: thinking Xavier and He are two interchangeable names. Xavier goes with tanh and sigmoid, He with the ReLU family.

p21-pca-steps-title.name: p21-pca-steps-title
p21-pca-steps-title.text: From image patches to data rows: the steps of PCA initialization

p21-pca-steps-ctx.name: p21-pca-steps-ctx
p21-pca-steps-ctx.text: The third route uses no random numbers but learns from data first. Let the stride be $s$.

p21-pca-steps-s0-t.name: p21-pca-steps-s0-t
p21-pca-steps-s0-t.text: Cut many $s\times s$ patches from images and flatten each into a vector.

p21-pca-steps-s1-t.name: p21-pca-steps-s1-t
p21-pca-steps-s1-t.text: Shift each patch by a few pixels and collect the shifted patches too (to make the features steadier under small shifts).

p21-pca-steps-s2-t.name: p21-pca-steps-s2-t
p21-pca-steps-s2-t.text: Treat all patches as the rows of a data matrix and do principal component analysis.

p21-pca-steps-s3-t.name: p21-pca-steps-s3-t
p21-pca-steps-s3-t.text: Each eigenvector arranged back to $s\times s$ is one initial convolution kernel. Repeating layer by layer can initialize a whole CNN.

p21-pca-steps-pca-t.name: p21-pca-steps-pca-t
p21-pca-steps-pca-t.text: PCA finds the 'directions of greatest variation' in the data: the first eigenvector has the most variation, the second is the largest among the remaining directions, and so on, mutually perpendicular.

p21-pca-steps-sz-t.name: p21-pca-steps-sz-t
p21-pca-steps-sz-t.text: An $s\times s$ patch has $s^{2}$ dimensions and PCA gives $s^{2}$ eigenvectors (matrix size $s^{2}\times s^{2}$); each eigenvector arranged back to $s\times s$ is one kernel. This is our interpretation of the source and is marked.

p22-pca-result-title.name: p22-pca-result-title
p22-pca-result-title.text: Nine native small kernels: which direction explains the most variation?

p22-pca-result-ctx.name: p22-pca-result-ctx
p22-pca-result-ctx.text: Experiment [Added]: a $64\times64$ synthetic image, $s=3$, original patches plus patches shifted by $1$ cell down, right and diagonally, $4\times20\times20=1600$ patches in all (each $9$-dimensional).

image.alt: The nine 3×3 kernels from PCA; colours show sign, titles show the share of variance

p22-pca-result-k1-t.name: p22-pca-result-k1-t
p22-pca-result-k1-t.text: The $1$st: all nine cells one colour, the 'averaging' kernel, $91.5\%$ of the variance — most of this image's variation is overall brightness.

p22-pca-result-k2-t.name: p22-pca-result-k2-t
p22-pca-result-k2-t.text: The $2$nd and $3$rd: up–down contrast and left–right contrast, i.e. horizontal and vertical edge detectors.

p22-pca-result-k3-t.name: p22-pca-result-k3-t
p22-pca-result-k3-t.text: The remaining six: messy shapes, each under $0.6\%$, mostly catching noise.

p22-pca-result-note-t.name: p22-pca-result-note-t
p22-pca-result-note-t.text: The shares depend on this synthetic image; another image would differ. Advantage: the kernels' start already carries data structure; drawbacks: an extra PCA, awkward to repeat layer by layer, rarely the default in modern practice, which usually uses He and Xavier.

p23-practice-xh-title.name: p23-practice-xh-title
p23-practice-xh-title.text: Your turn: compute standard deviations and pick the dimensions that are accurate enough

p23-practice-xh-q1-t.name: p23-practice-xh-q1-t
p23-practice-xh-q1-t.text: 1. $n_{\mathrm{in}}=n_{\mathrm{out}}=256$: compute the Xavier and He standard deviations.

p23-practice-xh-q2-t.name: p23-practice-xh-q2-t
p23-practice-xh-q2-t.text: 2. $n_{\mathrm{in}}=784$, $n_{\mathrm{out}}=100$: compute the Xavier and He standard deviations.

p23-practice-xh-q3-t.name: p23-practice-xh-q3-t
p23-practice-xh-q3-t.text: 3. In the experiment of Section 3, to get the maximum relative distance error below $0.15$, which of the four dimensions ($10,50,100,400$) work?

p23-practice-xh-a1-t.name: p23-practice-xh-a1-t
p23-practice-xh-a1-t.text:
Xavier $=\sqrt{2/512}=0.0625$; He $=\sqrt{2/256}=0.0884$.
He is $\sqrt2$ times Xavier (it divides only by the fan-in).

p23-practice-xh-a2-t.name: p23-practice-xh-a2-t
p23-practice-xh-a2-t.text: Xavier $=0.0476$ (denominator $884$); He $=0.0505$ (denominator $784$). The two are close.

p23-practice-xh-a3-t.name: p23-practice-xh-a3-t
p23-practice-xh-a3-t.text:
Maximum errors $0.69,\ 0.30,\ 0.24,\ 0.13$.
Only $k=400$ is below $0.15$; the $0.24$ of $k=100$ is not enough.

p24-misconceptions-title.name: p24-misconceptions-title
p24-misconceptions-title.text: What is wrong with these four statements?

p24-misconceptions-ctx.name: p24-misconceptions-ctx
p24-misconceptions-ctx.text: Judge each one first, then read the correction on the right.

p24-misconceptions-c0-t.name: p24-misconceptions-c0-t
p24-misconceptions-c0-t.text: The gradients are also $0$ or perfectly symmetric, and the network cannot learn.

p24-misconceptions-m1-t.name: p24-misconceptions-m1-t
p24-misconceptions-m1-t.text: 'The larger the weights the better, so nothing vanishes.'

p24-misconceptions-c1-t.name: p24-misconceptions-c1-t
p24-misconceptions-c1-t.text: Too large also blows up, and tanh saturates.

p24-misconceptions-c2-t.name: p24-misconceptions-c2-t
p24-misconceptions-c2-t.text: Xavier goes with tanh and sigmoid; He with ReLU.

p24-misconceptions-c3-t.name: p24-misconceptions-c3-t
p24-misconceptions-c3-t.text: It only says a random start does not destroy the distance structure — it speaks of the start, not the end.

p25-quiz-a-ctx.name: p25-quiz-a-ctx
p25-quiz-a-ctx.text: The source's questions with all options; the source page marks no answers, and the answers and explanations are written from this unit ([Added]).

p25-quiz-a-q0-t.name: p25-quiz-a-q0-t
p25-quiz-a-q0-t.text:
Why must a CNN be initialized before backpropagation?
A. Convolution kernels are not weights, so no gradient can be computed
B. The weights are the kernel values; backprop is iterative optimization, and without initial values there is no variable to optimize
C. Initialization can fully replace the loss function
D. He initialization makes training unnecessary

p25-quiz-a-a0-t.name: p25-quiz-a-a0-t
p25-quiz-a-a0-t.text: Answer B. The kernel numbers are the weights (A is wrong); initialization cannot replace the loss (C is wrong), nor can He initialization make training unnecessary (D is wrong). See Section 1.

p25-quiz-a-q1-t.name: p25-quiz-a-q1-t
p25-quiz-a-q1-t.text:
What is the relation between random initialization and the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma?
A. JL requires all weights to be 0
B. Weights can be viewed as a random projection, and JL says a random projection approximately preserves pairwise distances
C. JL applies only to second-order Newton methods
D. JL forbids ReLU

p25-quiz-a-a1-t.name: p25-quiz-a-a1-t
p25-quiz-a-a1-t.text: Answer B. A layer's weights are a projection matrix; JL is unrelated to all-zero weights, Newton's method and ReLU. See Section 3.

p26-quiz-b-ctx.name: p26-quiz-b-ctx
p26-quiz-b-ctx.text: The source's questions with all options; the source page marks no answers, and the answers and explanations are written from this unit ([Added]).

p26-quiz-b-q0-t.name: p26-quiz-b-q0-t
p26-quiz-b-q0-t.text:
Which is correct about initial value size and modern initialization methods?
A. The larger the weights the better, to avoid explosion
B. Too large explodes, too small vanishes; Xavier/Glorot suits tanh/sigmoid, He suits ReLU
C. Xavier is designed for ReLU, He for sigmoid
D. Modern networks must use plain uniform $[-100,100]$ initialization

p26-quiz-b-a0-t.name: p26-quiz-b-a0-t
p26-quiz-b-a0-t.text: Answer B. A is wrong in saying larger is better; C reverses the pairing; D is just an example that is far too large (Sections 2, 4).

p26-quiz-b-q1-t.name: p26-quiz-b-q1-t
p26-quiz-b-q1-t.text:
In unsupervised initialization, what does PCA produce to serve as convolution kernels?
A. A random Gaussian matrix, unrelated to patches
B. PCA on original and slightly shifted patches, giving an $s\times s$ eigenvector matrix as the initial kernels
C. An all-ones average-pooling kernel
D. Only biases, no kernels

p26-quiz-b-a1-t.name: p26-quiz-b-a1-t
p26-quiz-b-a1-t.text: Answer B. PCA on the original and slightly shifted patches; the eigenvectors arranged to s×s are the initial kernels (Section 5).

p27-summary-title.name: p27-summary-title
p27-summary-title.text: One sentence, plain words, formulas: what to take away from KP01

p27-summary-ctx.name: p27-summary-ctx
p27-summary-ctx.text: Close the slides and try to say the one-sentence version yourself.

p27-summary-one-t.name: p27-summary-one-t
p27-summary-one-t.text: Backpropagation is an iterative algorithm, so every weight must first get an initial value; the values should be random (to break symmetry) and their size adjusted by fan-in and fan-out, so that signals and gradients neither vanish nor explode across layers: He for ReLU, Xavier for tanh and sigmoid; alternatively learn a set of kernels from data with PCA first.

p27-summary-plain-t.name: p27-summary-plain-t
p27-summary-plain-t.text: Like a relay race for a group: every runner must start differently, or everyone does the same thing forever; the passing volume must be right — too soft and the back cannot hear, too loud and the back is deafened.

p27-summary-deep-t.name: p27-summary-deep-t
p27-summary-deep-t.text: The derivation assumes independent layer inputs, zero-mean weights and no biases, which real networks do not fully satisfy; so the standard deviation only 'roughly balances the start' and is not an exact guarantee. Example: He's green line rises to about $1.6$ in layers 8–9.

p27-summary-fix-t.name: p27-summary-fix-t
p27-summary-fix-t.text: Corrections and choices relative to the source: formulas, layer-by-layer experiments, the order of JL and its example are [Added]; the PCA matrix size $s^{2}\times s^{2}$ is an interpretation; the source does not discuss batch normalization and neither does this unit.

p27-summary-next-t.name: p27-summary-next-t
p27-summary-next-t.text: The start is set. But how do we know one architecture is better than another? The next unit (KP02) looks at ImageNet and AlexNet.

p01-start-nav.name: p01-start-nav
p01-start-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 01/27 · §1 Start · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p01-start-cue0.name: p01-start-cue0
p01-start-cue0.text: First a concrete kernel: these nine numbers are the weights the CNN has to learn.

p01-start-cue1.name: p01-start-cue1
p01-start-cue1.text: Backpropagation is iterative: every step starts from the 'current weights'.

p01-start-cue2.name: p01-start-cue2
p01-start-cue2.text: The right of the update formula needs W(0), so before the first step every weight must have an initial value.

p01-start-cue3.name: p01-start-cue3
p01-start-cue3.text: Three routes: random initialization, variance-aware Xavier and He, and learning from data with PCA; this unit answers them in turn.

p02-sym-forward-nav.name: p02-sym-forward-nav
p02-sym-forward-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 02/27 · §1 Symmetry: forward · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p02-sym-forward-cue0.name: p02-sym-forward-cue0
p02-sym-forward-cue0.text: First the network: the same input (1,2), and all weights of the two hidden neurons are 0.5.

p02-sym-forward-cue1.name: p02-sym-forward-cue1
p02-sym-forward-cue1.text: The two hidden neurons compute identical h: both 1.5.

p02-sym-forward-cue2.name: p02-sym-forward-cue2
p02-sym-forward-cue2.text: Output y=1.5, error −1.5; two identical hidden outputs added give no new feature.

p03-sym-backward-nav.name: p03-sym-backward-nav
p03-sym-backward-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 03/27 · §1 Symmetry: backward · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p03-sym-backward-cue2.name: p03-sym-backward-cue2
p03-sym-backward-cue2.text: Both neurons' input-weight gradients are also (−0.75, −1.5).

p03-sym-backward-cue3.name: p03-sym-backward-cue3
p03-sym-backward-cue3.text: Conclusion: they are forever two copies of one neuron; the extra one is wasted.

p04-zero-nav.name: p04-zero-nav
p04-zero-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 04/27 · §1 All zero · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p04-zero-cue0.name: p04-zero-cue0
p04-zero-cue0.text: Predict first: everything is 0 — what happens? Then look at the forward result.

p04-zero-cue1.name: p04-zero-cue1
p04-zero-cue1.text: Forward: hidden output 0, output 0, error −3, loss 4.5.

p04-zero-cue2.name: p04-zero-cue2
p04-zero-cue2.text: Backward: the output gradient is multiplied by the zero hidden output, the input gradient by the zero output weight — everything is 0.

p04-zero-cue3.name: p04-zero-cue3
p04-zero-cue3.text: So the starts must differ from each other: random numbers break the symmetry.

p05-practice-sym-nav.name: p05-practice-sym-nav
p05-practice-sym-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 05/27 · Practice · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p05-practice-sym-cue0.name: p05-practice-sym-cue0
p05-practice-sym-cue0.text: Think about the four questions first: output gradient, input gradient, next step, how to avoid symmetry.

p05-practice-sym-cue1.name: p05-practice-sym-cue1
p05-practice-sym-cue1.text: Answers: output gradients differ; input gradients are still equal in this step; they diverge only at the next step; the simplest fix is all-random weights.

p06-variance-nav.name: p06-variance-nav
p06-variance-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 06/27 · §2 Refresher · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p06-variance-cue0.name: p06-variance-cue0
p06-variance-cue0.text: Rule 1: multiply by a and the variance is multiplied by a squared.

p06-variance-cue1.name: p06-variance-cue1
p06-variance-cue1.text: Rule 2: the variances of independent random numbers add.

p06-variance-cue2.name: p06-variance-cue2
p06-variance-cue2.text: Same known values: with Var(X)=4, scaling by 3 gives 36, an independent sum gives 8.

p06-variance-cue3.name: p06-variance-cue3
p06-variance-cue3.text: Reminder: enlarging the same variable and adding an independent one are different operations with different results (36 versus 8).

p07-selftest-nav.name: p07-selftest-nav
p07-selftest-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 07/27 · Practice · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p07-selftest-cue0.name: p07-selftest-cue0
p07-selftest-cue0.text: Answer the three questions yourself first.

p07-selftest-cue1.name: p07-selftest-cue1
p07-selftest-cue1.text: Answers: 50; max(0,z); the chain rule. If unsure, go back to the matching page or Weeks 2 and 3.

p08-rms-nav.name: p08-rms-nav
p08-rms-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 08/27 · §2 Measuring size · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p08-rms-cue0.name: p08-rms-cue0
p08-rms-cue0.text: rms is the square root of the mean of squares, measuring how large the signal is, without subtracting the mean.

p08-rms-cue1.name: p08-rms-cue1
p08-rms-cue1.text: Variance subtracts the mean first: Var = q − mean squared; the two are equal only when the mean is 0.

p08-rms-cue2.name: p08-rms-cue2
p08-rms-cue2.text: Substitute x=(0,2): rms=√2, but the variance is 1, not q=2.

p08-rms-cue3.name: p08-rms-cue3
p08-rms-cue3.text: The mean of ReLU outputs is often not 0, so we track rms and do not claim an exact halving of the variance.

p09-linear-nav.name: p09-linear-nav
p09-linear-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 09/27 · §2 Derivation 1 · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p09-linear-cue0.name: p09-linear-cue0
p09-linear-cue0.text: First expand: the square of a weighted sum has 'square terms' and 'cross terms'.

p09-linear-cue1.name: p09-linear-cue1
p09-linear-cue1.text: Square terms: each term's mean of squares is σ² times the input's mean of squares.

p09-linear-cue2.name: p09-linear-cue2
p09-linear-cue2.text: Cross terms: the weights are independent with mean 0, so the expectation cancels.

p09-linear-cue3.name: p09-linear-cue3
p09-linear-cue3.text: Only n square terms remain: mean of squares of the output = n σ² q.

p10-relu-half-nav.name: p10-relu-half-nav
p10-relu-half-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 10/27 · §2 Derivation 2 · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p10-relu-half-cue0.name: p10-relu-half-cue0
p10-relu-half-cue0.text: A symmetric set of z: red (negative) and blue (positive) come in pairs with the same squared size.

p10-relu-half-cue1.name: p10-relu-half-cue1
p10-relu-half-cue1.text: ReLU: negatives become 0, positives unchanged — the paired red half is taken away.

p10-relu-half-cue2.name: p10-relu-half-cue2
p10-relu-half-cue2.text: Half of the squared quantity is removed: the mean of squares is halved.

p10-relu-half-cue3.name: p10-relu-half-cue3
p10-relu-half-cue3.text: Square root: after one ReLU layer the rms is multiplied by √(n/2)·σ.

p11-factor-numbers-nav.name: p11-factor-numbers-nav
p11-factor-numbers-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 11/27 · §2 Numbers · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p11-factor-numbers-cue0.name: p11-factor-numbers-cue0
p11-factor-numbers-cue0.text: σ=0.01: factor 0.0707 per layer, after ten layers theory 3.1×10⁻¹², experiment 3.9×10⁻¹² — the signal shrinks to almost zero.

p11-factor-numbers-cue1.name: p11-factor-numbers-cue1
p11-factor-numbers-cue1.text: σ=1: factor 7.07 per layer, after ten layers theory 3.1×10⁸, experiment 3.9×10⁸ — the signal blows up.

p11-factor-numbers-cue2.name: p11-factor-numbers-cue2
p11-factor-numbers-cue2.text: Each layer differs only by a fixed factor, and ten layers multiplied differ by a dozen orders of magnitude; theory and experiment are of the same order.

p11-factor-numbers-cue3.name: p11-factor-numbers-cue3
p11-factor-numbers-cue3.text: Goal: a factor of about 1 per layer.

p12-relu-chart-nav.name: p12-relu-chart-nav
p12-relu-chart-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 12/27 · §2 ReLU layer by layer · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p12-relu-chart-cue0.name: p12-relu-chart-cue0
p12-relu-chart-cue0.text: First the red line: σ=0.01 falls all the way, almost zero after ten layers.

p12-relu-chart-cue1.name: p12-relu-chart-cue1
p12-relu-chart-cue1.text: Add the gold line: σ=1 shoots up, equally far from the green line (1), in the opposite direction.

p12-relu-chart-cue2.name: p12-relu-chart-cue2
p12-relu-chart-cue2.text: Add the green line: He's σ=0.141 sticks to 1.

p12-relu-chart-cue3.name: p12-relu-chart-cue3
p12-relu-chart-cue3.text: Add the blue line: Xavier with ReLU still shrinks layer by layer, because ReLU discards half the squared quantity each layer.

p13-tanh-nav.name: p13-tanh-nav
p13-tanh-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 13/27 · §2 tanh · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p13-tanh-cue0.name: p13-tanh-cue0
p13-tanh-cue0.text: Red line: tanh with σ=0.01 also drops to the 10⁻¹¹ range; when nearly linear it behaves like a linear layer.

p13-tanh-cue1.name: p13-tanh-cue1
p13-tanh-cue1.text: Gold line: σ=1 does not blow up but sticks near 0.96, because the tanh curve on the right squeezes the output into −1 to 1 and traps it in the flat part.

p13-tanh-cue2.name: p13-tanh-cue2
p13-tanh-cue2.text: Blue line: Xavier with tanh; after ten layers the rms is still 0.095 from a start of 0.1, almost unchanged.

p14-vanish-nav.name: p14-vanish-nav
p14-vanish-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 14/27 · §2 Consequences · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p14-vanish-cue0.name: p14-vanish-cue0
p14-vanish-cue0.text: Factor below 1: the signal shrinks layer by layer, and in the early layers it is almost gone.

p14-vanish-cue1.name: p14-vanish-cue1
p14-vanish-cue1.text: Factor above 1: the signal grows layer by layer.

p14-vanish-cue2.name: p14-vanish-cue2
p14-vanish-cue2.text: The backpropagated gradient passes the same chain of layers, so forward vanishing or exploding makes the gradient vanish or explode too.

p14-vanish-cue3.name: p14-vanish-cue3
p14-vanish-cue3.text: So 'the larger the weights the better' is wrong: too large is equally bad, and tanh saturates.

p15-practice-factor-nav.name: p15-practice-factor-nav
p15-practice-factor-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 15/27 · Practice · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p15-practice-factor-cue0.name: p15-practice-factor-cue0
p15-practice-factor-cue0.text: Work it out yourself: the factor, the ten-layer multiple, vanishing or exploding.

p15-practice-factor-cue1.name: p15-practice-factor-cue1
p15-practice-factor-cue1.text: Answers: factor 0.3536; 3.05×10⁻⁵ times after ten layers; it is vanishing.

p16-projection-nav.name: p16-projection-nav
p16-projection-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 16/27 · §3 Random projection · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p16-projection-cue0.name: p16-projection-cue0
p16-projection-cue0.text: Two different points through the same matrix give two new points.

p16-projection-cue1.name: p16-projection-cue1
p16-projection-cue1.text: Their difference vector is also multiplied by the same matrix; distance comes from this.

p16-projection-cue2.name: p16-projection-cue2
p16-projection-cue2.text: The random weights must have the right scale (variance 1/k), so that distances neither grow nor shrink overall.

p17-jl-nav.name: p17-jl-nav
p17-jl-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 17/27 · §3 JL lemma · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p17-jl-cue0.name: p17-jl-cue0
p17-jl-cue0.text: The lemma says the squared distance stays within a factor 1±ε, and the needed k is about ln N / ε².

p17-jl-cue1.name: p17-jl-cue1
p17-jl-cue1.text: The experiment measures distance directly, so the error is about half of ε; the two must not be mixed.

p17-jl-cue2.name: p17-jl-cue2
p17-jl-cue2.text: First the leftmost red bar: projecting to only 10 dimensions, the worst pair is off by 69%.

p17-jl-cue3.name: p17-jl-cue3
p17-jl-cue3.text: Raising the dimension to 50, 100, 400 lowers the maximum error to 30%, 24%, 13%: the trend is that larger k gives smaller error.

p18-he-nav.name: p18-he-nav
p18-he-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 18/27 · §4 He · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p18-he-cue0.name: p18-he-cue0
p18-he-cue0.text: Goal: make the output as large as the input, i.e. the factor per layer equals 1.

p18-he-cue1.name: p18-he-cue1
p18-he-cue1.text: Solve for σ: σ = √(2/n_in), which is He initialization, for the ReLU family.

p18-he-cue3.name: p18-he-cue3
p18-he-cue3.text: Experiment: over ten layers the rms lies between 0.99 and 1.62, and 1.24 at layer 10; note that standard deviation differs from variance, and this is not an exact guarantee.

p19-xavier-nav.name: p19-xavier-nav
p19-xavier-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 19/27 · §4 Xavier · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p19-xavier-cue0.name: p19-xavier-cue0
p19-xavier-cue0.text: Forward: tanh is nearly linear, factor √n_in·σ=1, so σ²=1/n_in.

p19-xavier-cue1.name: p19-xavier-cue1
p19-xavier-cue1.text: Backward: the gradient passes the fan-out and needs σ²=1/n_out.

p19-xavier-cue2.name: p19-xavier-cue2
p19-xavier-cue2.text: Xavier compromises: σ=√(2/(n_in+n_out)), serving both forward and backward.

p19-xavier-cue3.name: p19-xavier-cue3
p19-xavier-cue3.text: Three sets of numbers: both scale by fan-in and fan-out; the more n_in and n_out differ, the more the two differ.

p20-pairing-nav.name: p20-pairing-nav
p20-pairing-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 20/27 · §4 Pairing · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p20-pairing-cue0.name: p20-pairing-cue0
p20-pairing-cue0.text: Look at the top left first: He with ReLU, the layer-10 rms is about 1.24, the factor is exactly 1.

p20-pairing-cue1.name: p20-pairing-cue1
p20-pairing-cue1.text: Put Xavier on ReLU: factor 0.707, 0.031 after ten layers, slowly shrinking.

p20-pairing-cue2.name: p20-pairing-cue2
p20-pairing-cue2.text: Xavier with tanh is the matched pair: still 0.095 after ten layers, almost unchanged.

p20-pairing-cue3.name: p20-pairing-cue3
p20-pairing-cue3.text: The other way round, He on tanh: factor about √2, the signal grows and tanh is pushed to the flat part; so pairing matters.

p21-pca-steps-nav.name: p21-pca-steps-nav
p21-pca-steps-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 21/27 · §5 PCA · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p21-pca-steps-cue0.name: p21-pca-steps-cue0
p21-pca-steps-cue0.text: Step 1: cut s×s patches and flatten them into vectors.

p21-pca-steps-cue1.name: p21-pca-steps-cue1
p21-pca-steps-cue1.text: Step 2: collect the shifted patches too, making features steadier under small shifts.

p21-pca-steps-cue2.name: p21-pca-steps-cue2
p21-pca-steps-cue2.text: Step 3: treat all patches as data rows and do PCA to find the directions of greatest variation.

p21-pca-steps-cue3.name: p21-pca-steps-cue3
p21-pca-steps-cue3.text: Step 4: arrange the eigenvectors back to s×s as initial kernels; the matrix is s²×s² (our interpretation of the source).

p22-pca-result-nav.name: p22-pca-result-nav
p22-pca-result-nav.text: IDL 2026 FALL · Week 7 KP01 · 22/27 · §5 PCA result · Manual: Next to advance / Prev to go back; reveal answers after you try

p22-pca-result-cue0.name: p22-pca-result-cue0
